editorial.headline: Buttons, Zippers, and the Bali PMA Block
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 32907 covers the manufacture of buttons, zippers, and supporting components; nationally it is open to foreign ownership, but Bali blocks PMA registration.
editorial.body:
KBLI 32907 is a small industrial category with a practical role in garment, accessory, and product supply chains. The record defines it as the manufacture of various kinds of buttons, including hook buttons and press buttons, together with the manufacture of zippers and other supporting components. In plain English, this is not retail, tailoring, or fashion branding. It is the production side: the activity of making the fasteners and related parts that other businesses may later use in finished goods.

The scale position is broad. The record opens this activity to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar operators, so it can describe anything from a very small production setup to a larger industrial business, provided the activity remains within the stated manufacturing scope. That matters because the code is not framed around one narrow company size. It is an industrial activity that can be registered across every listed scale in the record.

Nationally, the foreign-investment picture is straightforward. The PMA status is TERBUKA, and the stated maximum foreign ownership is 100%, with the source given as Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. On the national reading alone, this is therefore a foreign-open activity with no lower ceiling shown in the record. A foreign investor looking only at the national PMA field would see a clean answer: the activity is open, and the foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%.

Bali changes the practical answer completely. The record marks this code as blocked in Bali, with the reason stated as: “OSS risk at scale Besar is Rendah/Menengah-Rendah on every scope → blocked by Bali moratorium 13 May 2026.” The moratorium rule is also explicit: Bali province blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanent. So the honest editorial conclusion is not that the code is partly open in Bali, or that Bali applies a separate percentage cap. It is that a foreigner cannot register this KBLI as a PMA in Bali today, even though the same activity is nationally marked TERBUKA with a 100% foreign-ownership ceiling.
